sourceInformation.source: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (Atari 2600, 1982), with the world and tone of the 1982 Steven Spielberg film written by Melissa Mathison
sourceInformation.genre: Stealth adventure with light puzzle and bicycle flight
sourceInformation.perspective: Elevated third-person exploration; trailing third-person flight
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js 0.180.0 WebGPURenderer, WebGPU with WebGL 2 compatibility, Rapier 0.19.3, Gamepad API, Web Audio, AI Hub session client 1.4.0, WebRTC, BroadcastChannel; esbuild 0.25.11 bundles the single HTML
sourceInformation.artDirection: Procedural stylized cel shading, ink outlines, miniature autumn suburb and redwood forest, indigo moonlight and warm windows
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer and authored AnimationClip keyframes for walking, sneaking, idle breathing, alien gestures and bicycle pedaling; procedural particles and effects
sourceInformation.audio: Original adaptive code-generated celesta, harp, pads and escape strings; synthesized effects, wind and crickets; Animalese-style gibberish voices; no audio files; music defaults to 10%
sourceInformation.online: 1–2 cooperative shared-world players via AI Hub; standalone WebRTC invitation/reply and same-browser rooms; local two-controller or keyboard-plus-controller co-op. Direct WebRTC has no TURN relay.
sourceInformation.testing: One-command scripted complete story, all 12 flight stars, failure/checkpoint/save, looping attract, live developer tools, emulated standard gamepads, phone/tablet touch profiles, file:// initialization, offline audio rendering, Rapier collision regressions, actual two-page co-op and official AI Hub harness at 150 ms latency / 50 ms jitter / 5% loss; Chromium WebGPU plus Xvfb WebGL 2 screenshots. Physical controllers, real touch hardware and human listening were unavailable.
sourceInformation.research: Original 1982 Atari instruction manual (AtariAge transcription): three communicator pieces, candy/energy, power zones, FBI/scientist pursuit, flower revival and forest rescue; official Amblin and Universal film descriptions, UCLA Film Archive and screenplay excerpt for film world, look, sound and bicycle escape; official Three.js/Rapier docs and AI Hub lib/hub docs/client

testingFeedback: 11 tracked product defects were corrected: 1 automated network-startup failure, 5 visual defects, and 5 co-op/input/save/menu issues found in integration and code review. Keyboard-menu assertions also exposed a parked-mouse test interference issue; the test now isolates keyboard navigation.
2 game-breaking co-op defects: server-only host player assignment and puzzle input without a local host player. A network startup race also blocked one AI Hub conformance scenario. All are fixed.

The complete scripted story and real two-page co-op flow, including every transmitter part, the shared signal, all 12 flight stars, and the ending; AI Hub standard/server/host-leave harness checks under latency, jitter and loss.
Headless WebGPU screenshots were blank on this workstation and gave no useful visual evidence; Xvfb with the WebGL 2 backend provided the visual checks.
engineFeedback: Three.js node toon materials and native AnimationMixer clips made the procedural ink world and expressive characters practical, with WebGPU and a WebGL 2 compatibility path.
I initially assumed a shared-world host always had a local player; AI Hub can use a server-only host. Headless WebGPU captures also required an Xvfb/WebGL visual fallback.
The host-authoritative adventure simulation, shared puzzle/input routing, controller-first UI, and procedural art and audio.
Coordinating first-frame shader warm-up, animation, physics and network readiness consistently across renderer backends.
none; no engine source was changed. The game uses the public Three.js and Rapier APIs.
A predictable first-frame preparation and headless image-capture path across WebGPU adapters and compatibility rendering.
promptFeedback: The emphasis on a complete emotional arc, controller-first play, procedural audio and a full vertical slice gave the game a clear identity.
The source title and year can refer to the Atari 2600 game or the film. I researched both, combining the game's communicator/candy/pursuit/rescue loop with the film's world and tone.
Making the entire story, touch and controller inputs, local co-op, standalone networking and AI Hub sessions work together in one portable HTML.
Specify a target playtime, identify whether the source names the film or its game adaptation, and say whether manual WebRTC invitation/reply exchange is preferred for standalone multiplayer.

aiHub.name: E.T. the Extra-Small Visitor
aiHub.tagline: A little friend. A very big night.
aiHub.description: Befriend a stranded visitor, borrow household treasures, and sneak past searching agents to build a call home. Then pedal into the moonlight in a warm, ink-drawn co-op adventure.
aiHub.controls: Left stick / WASD move; Cross / E help; Circle / Shift sneak; Square / C candy; Triangle / F heartlight; R2 / Space pedal; right stick / mouse drag camera; Options / Esc pause; touch drag and contextual help.
